title: TextGen API live intro — streams, params, idempotency & retries
summary: Intro demo of Redwood hosted TextGen/chat API focusing on streaming behavior, tuning parameters and production retry/idempotency patterns. Discussed latency vs cost, idempotency keys, console quick tour, and security basics (SOC2, SSO, data retention). Agreed next steps: run a short pilot benchmark, share security pack, and schedule SE-led POC scoping call.

transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone — thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood. We'll do a short live demo of our TextGen/chat hosted API, focus on streaming behavior and then go over retries and idempotency. Priya will show some console bits.
[00:18] Alicia Gomez: Thanks, Jordan. We're mostly interested in low-latency chat for triage assistants — want to understand how streaming behaves with short tokens and partial outputs.
[00:30] Priya Nair: Cool, I'll jump into the console in a minute. Quick outline: 1) live stream demo, 2) param tuning (temperature/max tokens/presence penalties), 3) retry and idempotency patterns, 4) quick Q&A.
[00:46] Dev Patel: One thing up front — our SLA target is under 250ms tail for 95% of 1-2 sentence responses. Is that realistic on hosted?
[00:58] Jordan Lee: Short answer: yes for many models, depends on model size and batching. For hosted we publish verified latencies but you can also reserve Dedicated for hard SLOs. We'll show how you can trade cost vs latency.
[01:12] Priya Nair: Alright demo — opening the console. Note: this is the hosted TextGen endpoint. I'm sending a streaming request with an idempotency key. Watch the partial tokens come through — they arrive as SSE events, you'll see chunks every 40–60ms for short responses.
[01:30] [screen noise / brief typing]
[01:38] Priya Nair: (typing) Sending prompt: "Triage steps for patient with mild chest pain, non-emergent." Ok, we got a partial first chunk: "Start with vitals, en...," then next chunk completes to "...and consider ECG if persistent." You can read and display interim tokens to give users faster feedback.
[01:58] Hannah Cho: Is the partial text deterministic order? We had issues with chunk reordering in older infra.
[02:04] Priya Nair: Good question. The stream preserves generation order from the model; however, network retries can cause duplicate or delayed chunks. We include sequence offsets on events — apologies if the console truncates that — the SDK surfaces chunk offsets so you can dedupe.
[02:22] Dev Patel: How do you recommend handling a client disconnect mid-stream?
[02:27] Priya Nair: Two patterns: 1) idempotent retries — use an idempotency key per logical user request so replays don't create different outputs, 2) server-side caching of prefix tokens — Redwood supports prefix/KV cache on compatible models to resume quickly. We can show a small example with cache hits.
[02:44] Samir Rao: Security question — data retention for hosted: can we opt out of storage? We can't retain PHI beyond ephemeral processing.
[02:51] Jordan Lee: Yes — hosted has configurable retention tiers. For regulated PHI-heavy workloads we'd normally recommend Private or on-prem, but we do offer short retention + encryption at rest with customer-managed keys in some plans. We'll send SOC2 and KMS notes.
[03:08] Priya Nair: Back to retries. Here's a typical client retry pattern: client sends a POST with an idempotency-key header. If an error like 5xx occurs, retry with same key and idempotency header; Redwood will either return a cached response or re-run generation deterministically when supported. Also we recommend exponential backoff with jitter — typical base is 200ms.
[03:31] Alicia Gomez: Is generation deterministic with same key? If the underlying model is nondeterministic, how do you guarantee same response?
[03:38] Priya Nair: Good nuance — for temperature>0 you can't guarantee identical tokens. For deterministic replays we recommend zero temperature + fixed top_p or use cached results from a prior successful call. Idempotency here ensures you don't create duplicate side-effects, not that you'll get identical text for non-deterministic sampling.
[03:58] Dev Patel: How about partial token billing — we need cost estimates for streaming vs non-streaming.
[04:03] Jordan Lee: Billing is per generated token; streaming doesn't change units but it can influence latency which impacts throughput and thus cost for concurrent usage. Our Optimize product can run simulations and recommend quantization/model families to reduce unit cost. We'll include a sample cost calc.
[04:20] [00:04:20] Priya Nair: Quick SDK snippet: (paraphrased) client.generate({model: 'rwd-medium-8k', stream: true, temperature: 0.3, max_tokens: 120, idempotency_key: 'user123-req-456'}) — then in the stream handler dedupe by chunk.offset and apply backpressure on the UI.
[04:40] Hannah Cho: Can we set server-side timeouts? Sometimes our app needs a 300ms hard timeout.
[04:45] Jordan Lee: You can configure request-level timeout and Redwood will abort on the server; the SDK surfaces that. For hard SLOs we recommend Dedicated or pinned model variants to avoid noisy neighbor latency spikes.
[04:58] Priya Nair: I'm switching to a simulated error to show retry flow. I'll trigger a transient 502 from the sandbox. (typing) Client sees 502, retry after backoff, same idempotency key, second call either returns cached response or new one depending on prior success. Observe the console log shows "replay returned cached result".
[05:18] Dev Patel: Nice. Any best practices for chunk-assembly on mobile where bandwidth is flaky?
[05:23] Priya Nair: For mobile: assemble chunks client-side but show partials only after a small debounce (50–100ms) to avoid UI jitter. Also include a checksum or offset to detect missing segments and request a short resume token, Redwood can re-emit last N tokens if you include the resume_id.
[05:40] Alicia Gomez: You mentioned KV cache — is that per-customer or shared?
[05:44] Priya Nair: Cache is tenant-isolated for hosted customers. You can also configure prefix caching expiration. For chat apps caching common system prompts or static context is a big win.
[05:55] Samir Rao: What about encryption and key management? We need to know if we can bring our own keys.
[05:59] Jordan Lee: For hosted we offer BYOK through KMS integrations on enterprise tiers. We'll share the KMS integration guide. For strict compliance, Private or on-prem is the path.
[06:12] [06:12] Priya Nair: Quick note on parameters — temperature controls randomness; top_p controls nucleus sampling. For short triage answers we recommend low temp (0.0–0.3) and top_p around 0.8 if you want a little variation. Presence and frequency penalties can reduce hallucination for repetitive notes.
[06:33] Dev Patel: Do you have a recommended default for chat message history size? We want to keep context but not blow request sizes.
[06:39] Priya Nair: We see teams keep 2–4 recent user turns + a condensed system summary. Redwood Console has a context summarizer tool in Optimize that periodically compresses long histories into short summaries to keep token usage down.
[06:52] Hannah Cho: Is function-calling supported in streams? We want structured JSON back from model.
[06:58] Priya Nair: Yes — function calling can be streamed; you'll get stream tokens that build up the JSON and then an end-of-stream event with the final parse. The SDK includes a helper to assemble and validate the JSON. A caveat: if you set temperature high it may be more noisy, so keep generation deterministic for structured outputs.
[07:18] Samir Rao: Any network requirements or firewall rules we should plan for?
[07:22] Jordan Lee: If using hosted, you'll call public endpoints over TLS. For higher security we support IP allowlists and VPC peering in enterprise plans. We'll include a firewall checklist.
[07:33] Alicia Gomez: What's the quickest way to prove latency for us? We want a focused bench for 95th percentile under 250ms.
[07:39] Jordan Lee: We propose a 24–48 hour pilot: you run ~5k realistic short prompts via our sandbox token with our SE monitoring. Priya will work with Dev on the payloads; we'll collect latency histograms and tuning recommendations.
[07:52] Dev Patel: Sounds good. Can Optimize recommend smaller quantized model variants if latency is an issue?
[07:56] Priya Nair: Yes — Optimize runs workload profiling and suggests model families and quantization levels (4-bit/8-bit) and batching configs. For streaming small responses you might prefer a quantized small-medium model to hit low tail latency.
[08:10] [08:10] Hannah Cho: Any particular gotchas for telemetry and observability? We need token-level cost breakdown and per-route latency.
[08:15] Jordan Lee: Console has per-route dashboards, token cost breakdown, traces and sampling. We also provide hooks for distributed tracing (zipkin/opentelemetry) to tie requests back to your app.
[08:29] Alicia Gomez: Ok, let's cover next steps and who owns what.
[08:33] Jordan Lee: Recap: 1) Jordan will send pricing and the security pack; 2) Priya will share retry/idempotency runbook and a small SDK example for mobile; 3) BrightLeaf to send sample prompts for pilot. Proposed pilot start is 2026-04-26.
[08:49] Dev Patel: I'll try to get the sample payloads by end of week.
[08:52] Samir Rao: Please include SOC2 cert and the KMS BYOK steps in the security pack.
[08:58] Jordan Lee: Will do. Any final quick questions?
[09:02] Hannah Cho: Not from me. Thanks, that was helpful.
[09:05] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with links. Demo recording and notes will be in the calendar invite.
[09:10] [END]
